definition: The logogen model of 1969 is a model of speech recognition that uses units called "logogens" to explain how humans comprehend spoken or written words.
details: Logogens are a vast number of specialized recognition units, each able to recognize one specific word. This model provides for the effects of context on word recognition.

explainer.lead: The logogen model, proposed in 1969, is a model of speech recognition built on units called logogens. It matters as an early account of how context shapes human word recognition.

tiers.eli5: It is like having a huge set of light switches, one per word, each flicking on when enough clues for that word arrive.
tiers.practitioner: Cognitive scientists use the model to explain contextual priming effects in word recognition experiments. A pitfall is that it is a psychological model of human processing, not an engineering recipe for building recognizers.
tiers.paperLevel: Each logogen is a specialized recognition unit for one specific word, accumulating evidence until a threshold is reached; the model accounts for context effects on recognition but is a behavioural account rather than a precise computational formula.

explainer.example: Hearing the start of a sentence primes the logogens for likely upcoming words, so a word matching context is recognized faster than one that does not.
